Adult Northern smoothtongue (Leuroglossus schmidti) in the Bering Sea region typically reach a maximum standard length of 20 centimeters [Li = 20 centimeters], a size that is comparable to other mesopelagic planktivores inhabiting subarctic waters. Females at this ultimate size attain a wet weight of 43.8 grams [Wwi = 43.8 grams], representing the upper end of the species' body mass distribution. In contrast, newly emerged prolarvae, having absorbed their yolk reserves but not yet commenced exogenous feeding, have an extremely small wet weight at birth of only 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams], a value derived from the roughly 0.8 millimeter diameter of the pelagic egg. This dramatic disparity between neonatal and adult mass underscores the extensive growth trajectory this species undergoes during its development through the larval and juvenile stages.

The onset of reproductive maturity in Leuroglossus schmidti occurs at a standard length of approximately 10 centimeters [Lp = approximately 10 centimeters], at which point individuals attain a corresponding wet weight at puberty of approximately 5.6 grams [Wwp = approximately 5.6 grams]. Morphological indicators of gonadal development become apparent at this size threshold, with vitellogenesis initiating in females and spermatogenesis beginning in males. This size at maturity is considerably smaller than the asymptotic length, indicating a substantial period of continued somatic growth after reproductive capacity is first achieved, a pattern common among iteroparous teleosts that prioritize early reproduction alongside continued body size increase. Field collections suggest that individuals require several years to reach this pubertal size under the cold thermal conditions typical of their habitat.

Under the persistently cold water temperatures of approximately 3.1 °C [T = 3.1 °C] that characterize the species' deep pelagic habitat, reproductive output is constrained by the slow metabolic rates typical of this thermal regime. Females produce on average 7.9 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 7.9 eggs per spawning event] and are capable of spawning once daily [F_R_i = once daily] during the breeding season, yielding a maximum daily reproductive rate of 7.9 eggs per day [Ri = 7.9 eggs per day]. This remarkable spawning frequency is unusual for a bathypelagic fish and likely reflects an adaptation to low encounter rates with mates and high egg mortality in the deep scattering layer environment. The capacity for daily spawning is contingent upon adequate lipid reserves accumulated during the preceding feeding season.

The lifespan of Leuroglossus schmidti has been estimated from otolith microincrement analysis to be approximately 5.5 years [am = approximately 5.5 years] under the ambient temperature conditions of 3.1 °C [T = 3.1 °C] typical of its depth distribution. This longevity is consistent with that of other small mesopelagic fishes that experience low predation pressure and reduced metabolic costs in the cold, dark waters of the subarctic Pacific. Age validation using known-age captive specimens has confirmed that growth increments are deposited daily at this temperature, providing a reliable method for estimating individual age and correlating it with size-at-age data for population assessment. The species appears to exhibit negligible senescence until the final year of life.
